Euler limit

Words: 121 Articles: 1
Viscous fluid flow OurBigBook.com
The Euler limit sends the kinematic viscosity to zero while observing the flow at a fixed positive distance from a wall. If the velocity and its derivatives remain regular there, the viscous term disappears and the outer flow obeys the Euler equations for an inviscid fluid. No penetration remains the wall condition for the outer problem; tangential no slip is enforced in a separate viscous boundary layer and cannot generally be imposed on the inviscid outer flow.

Inviscid core

Words: 54
Euler limit OurBigBook.com
An inviscid core is the part of a high-Reynolds number flow outside thin wall or shear layers, where viscosity is negligible at the retained asymptotic order. It obeys the Euler equations for an inviscid fluid. Its tangential velocity need not satisfy no slip at a material wall; adjoining viscous boundary layers supply that condition and can influence the core through displacement and pressure matching.

Pressure-driven channel flow (μΔ⊥​w=−G)

Words: 122 Articles: 1
Viscous fluid flow OurBigBook.com
A steady unidirectional incompressible viscous flow in a rigid channel, driven by G=−dp/dz, reduces the axial momentum equation to the displayed Poisson equation, with w=0 on the cross-sectional boundary. Circular-pipe flow is the Hagen-Poiseuille flow special case; an arbitrary cross section need not have that parabolic radial profile.

Corner expansion of pressure-driven sector flow (λn​=(2n+1)π/(2α))

Words: 77
Pressure-driven channel flow OurBigBook.com
In a symmetric wedge ∣θ∣<α, a constant Poisson forcing admits the particular solution r2(cos2θ/cos2α−1)/4, except at resonant angles. Zero-wall harmonic corrections have exponents λn​=(2n+1)π/(2α). If the smallest exponent is below two, the global boundary data make that homogeneous mode dominate the local quadratic forcing. If it is below one, the velocity gradient can be singular although the velocity vanishes. When an exponent equals two, the appropriate radial solution contains r2logr, since Δ(r2logrcos2θ)=4cos2θ.

Symmetric viscous interaction in an indented Poiseuille channel

Words: 135 Articles: 1
Plane Poiseuille flow OurBigBook.com
At large Reynolds number R, a long indentation of relative height ϵ has nonlinear near-wall interaction when the streamwise scale ratio satisfies λ/R=ϵ3. The regime R1/7≪λ≪R gives a thin viscous layer and an effectively common pressure across the core. The core displacement is u1​=A(x)U0′​(y) and v1​=−A′(x)U0​(y). A lower wall displaced to ϵF(x) produces layer displacement F+A, while the upper wall produces −A. Uniqueness for their common pressure forcing and upstream data makes the two layer displacements equal, so A=−F/2.

One-third-power similarity of an indented channel boundary layer (G′′′+32​GG′′−31​(G′)2=32​pˉ​)

Words: 49
Symmetric viscous interaction in an indented Poiseuille channel OurBigBook.com
For indentation F=bx1/3, the common layer displacement is H=bx1/3/2. The boundary layer stream function ψ=x2/3G(zx−1/3) gives velocity U=x1/3G′ and pressure P=pˉ​x2/3. Substitution into the Prandtl boundary-layer equation yields the displayed equation, with G(0)=G′(0)=0 and G′∼6η+3b. This is a conditional similarity construction: the constant pˉ​ must permit a solution of the boundary value problem.

Two-layer plane Poiseuille flow with unequal viscosities (u±​=U0​+Cy/μ±​−Gy2/(2μ±​))

Words: 99
Plane Poiseuille flow OurBigBook.com
Two viscous layers occupy −a<y<0 and 0<y<a, with viscosities μ−​ and μ+​. A uniform driving pressure gradient G=−px​>0, a stationary flat interface and no-slip outer walls give the displayed plane Poiseuille flow, where U0​=Ga2/(μ−​+μ+​) and C=Ga(μ−​−μ+​)/[2(μ−​+μ+​)]. These constants follow from continuity of velocity and shear stress at the interface and zero wall velocities. The upper-to-lower volume-flux ratio is (1+7r)/[r(7+r)], with r=μ+​/μ−​. As r→∞, the interface becomes effectively stationary, the upper flux vanishes, and the lower layer approaches flow between two stationary plates a distance a apart. The upper wall stress remains finite despite its vanishing velocity gradient.

Fully developed flow (u=u(z)x^)

Words: 61
Viscous fluid flow OurBigBook.com
A fully developed parallel flow has a velocity profile independent of the streamwise coordinate. In a planar channel a representative profile is u=u(z)x^; wall conditions and translational symmetry remove cross-stream motion. The coefficient κ is thermal diffusivity, and the boundary coefficient α is normalized accordingly.

The hz​ term destabilizes long waves through the Rayleigh–Plateau instability, whereas hzzz​ damps short waves. The linear growth rate is (k2−k4)/3−iGk, with fastest growth at ∣k∣=1/2​. The gravity parameter is G=ρga2/(γϵ) when film thickness is scaled as ϵah and axial distance by cylinder radius a.

Its real positive exponent gives a monotone trailing approach and its complex stable exponents give damped capillary waves ahead, with physical wavelength 4πa/(35/6c1/3). Zero-liquid-flux surfactant film (Q=0)

The lower part of the liquid flows backwards while the surface and upper third flow forwards. Clean-sheet long-wave rupture plateau (limk→0, k=0​s=3V/(4μh03​))
Words: 63
Van der Waals rupture instability of a viscous sheet OurBigBook.com
A sheet with stress-free surfaces supports nearly uniform cross-thickness extensional motion. Its diverging long-wave mobility compensates the weak pressure gradient, leaving the nonzero rate limit in the creeping-flow model. The exactly uniform thickness change is excluded at fixed volume, and unsteady inertia or finite domain size can regularize the limiting prediction. Strong surfactant immobilization instead makes the rate vanish quadratically with wave number.

Capillary closure of a falling hollow thread
Words: 83
Capillary tensile force of a hollow slender thread OurBigBook.com
For steady equal-pressure flow, mass conservation gives Aw=A0​w0​ and the kinematic boundary condition gives (Dw​)z​=γ/(2μw​), where D=Re​−Ri​. Therefore finite-height closure occurs exactly when
2μw0​​γ​∫0z∗​​w(z)​dz​=A0​​−D0​.
(64)
For positive velocity the integral is increasing. If it diverges, closure is finite; if its limiting value lies below the right-hand threshold, there is no finite closure. Quadratic freely falling profiles have logarithmically divergent integrals, while sufficiently strongly drawn exponentially accelerating profiles can have finite integrals. Thus nozzle speed alone is insufficient to guarantee closure: the axial tension or downstream condition matters.
